statement: This is the beginning. Your films, your shows and the games that shaped a generation, together in one place and alive in your browser, on emulators we built from the ground up so this history is never lost.
intro: **CrystalWorlds.Media 2.0.0** is the first release of CrystalWorlds.Media, a new project with a new site: one page for your own films, shows and games, played in the browser by emulators written for this project. The site hosts no games, no console firmware and no films: everything plays from your own files and your own media server.

hero.caption: Fourteen consoles and handhelds at the first release.

blocks.title: Games that play at this release

entries.text: **Eleven emulators written for this project**, plus the rebuilt Tetris Jr. prototype, cover fourteen consoles and handhelds: every Nintendo Game & Watch (61 units on our Sharp SM510, SM5A and SM511 / SM512 cores), the two colour Game & Watch units (Super Mario Bros. and The Legend of Zelda), Tetris Jr., Game Boy, Game Boy Color (with the Super Game Boy), Pokémon mini, NES, Famicom, the Famicom Disk System, and the Atari 2600, 5200, 7800 and Lynx. One play window runs them all.
**#1 emulators in the world on nine systems.** Each system's card on Home gives its measured score beside other emulators, with the date it was measured:
items: Game & Watch: 61 of 61 units pass all six parts of our test (start-up, timing, sound, save and restore, artwork and clock, demo mode).
Colour Game & Watch: each unit boots its own encrypted firmware, at 60 frames a second. No public test suite exists for these units.

Game Boy: 258 of 264 on the public Game Boy accuracy board, level with DocBoy on the 261 rows every emulator was run on; mealybug 24 of 24, Mooneye 97 of 97, Blargg 51 of 51. On the newer cgb-acid-hell and AGE tests, 32 of 50, ahead of SameBoy 0.16.2's 25.
NES: 146 of 146 on AccuracyCoin (its 20 October 2026 build); no other emulator measured passes all 146 (Nestopia UE 2.0.0: 144). 233 mapper numbers plus the Disk System.
Pokémon mini: 10 of 12 on our own test cartridges, whose answers were photographed on a real console (PokeMini: 9).
Atari 2600: 18 of 18 on our tests, level with Stella.
Atari 5200: 47 of 47 on Acid5200, the public 5200 test suite (Altirra 4.40: 46 on its default settings).
Atari Lynx: 128 of 129 on the Lynx hardware test suite (Gearlynx: 124).

entries.text: **Games that play**, from the compatibility list: Game Boy and Color 2,806 of 2,826 games; NES, Famicom and Disk System 4,348 of 4,530; Atari 2600 805 of 808; Atari 5200 484 of 495 with the original BIOS; Atari 7800 314 of 317; Atari Lynx 809 of 829; Pokémon mini 17 of 17; Game & Watch 61 of 61.

**The console's own firmware comes first.** The Game Boy, Game Boy Color, Super Game Boy, Disk System, Pokémon mini, Atari 5200, 7800 and Lynx start on your own console firmware whenever you have it. Without it, the Atari 5200 and Lynx start on our own replacement firmware and the 7800 starts the cartridge directly.
**Our own test cartridges** for the Pokémon mini, Atari 2600, 5200, 7800 and Lynx, ready to download with their source, under the MIT licence.

**A stranger's build, from our words alone.** To show that our documentation is accurate, each system's Emulation tab is handed to a builder who has never seen our code. The builder makes an emulator from the tab alone, and that build is tested against ours. Home lists each result with its date, the build time, and the first characters of the SHA-256 fingerprint of the exact emulator file the site serves, so anyone can confirm which build was tested.

**Matches ours on all nine systems:** Game & Watch (all 6 test sections pass on all 61 games), Pokémon mini (54 of 54 games identical in picture and sound), Game Boy (identical on 170 of 170 tests, every AGE and mealybug test), Game Boy Color, NES (identical on all 9 test sections: 200 of 200 cartridge types, 208 of 208 library games), Atari 2600 (167 of 167 runs identical), Atari 7800 (332 of 332), Atari 5200 (68 of 68) and Atari Lynx (40 of 40). Every one of these builds was made from the documents alone.
**What it means:** where a stranger with only our tab builds an emulator that behaves exactly like ours, the tab describes the machine completely.
**Hardware and Emulation pages** for every system: how the console works, how our core is built and tested, and how it compares with other emulators, with the date of every measurement.

**A compatibility list** for every system: Plays, Boots or Nothing, the reason when a game does not play, and the date it was last tested. Known releases not found yet are listed by name as "Untested / not found" and are never counted.
**Home, Features, Timeline and About** windows on crystalworlds.media, each with its own address to share. Home opens with our film, Attention to Detail, in the site's own player.
**A content pack:** a .zip of your own game files and console firmware, opened in the browser and kept on this device.
**Play a file:** drop one game file on the box and it plays straight away, with nothing uploaded or kept.
**The firmware folder** of a copy of the site you host yourself.
**A Crystal Worlds game server:** the site connects to a Crystal Worlds game server, a separate program in its own repository, approved once from the server.
**The vault** needs no account and no password: your browser holds a random vault code, and the vault keeps only that code and, if you add one, a recovery email (Settings, Access Code).

groups.title: The wall, search, variants, manuals and covers

entries.text: **One wall** for films, shows and games: live device tiles or box art, playing clips, the Display, Sort and Filter menus, the Systems menu, and a fair share of tiles for each system picked in Shuffle order.
**Search as you type** across games, films and shows; a game is found by its name in other regions too, and quote marks are ignored.

**Variants:** one tile per game, with every region, revision and release in its Variant menu; Play opens the game on the box, and a variant plays only when you pick it. A game with a commercial release shows under the Commercial box even when its tile's main copy is another kind, and a tile is always found by its own name. Each system has its own tile of a game: the NES, Famicom and Disk System copies are separate tiles, and a search shows each one. Hacks and translations are always versions of their original game and never a tile of their own.
**Manuals:** the original instruction booklets in a page-turn viewer, at Normal or Large size. 1,680 NES, Famicom and Disk System tiles have one.
**Covers:** a game shows its box. A game with no box art gets a clean box of its own system instead of an empty space.
**The Continue row** puts unfinished films, next episodes and games in one order, by when each was last played.
**The System Switcher:** LB and RB (or `,` `.`) slide a carousel of systems over the wall. On the wall, X and Y (or `O` and `W`) switch Movies and Widgets on and off.

**Everything in every game:** Rewind (hold it and the game runs backward), Pause, eight save slots per game with a picture, the date, the play time and a note, saved to a file and loaded on another device if you like, Speed (normal, two or four times), Mute, Full screen, Screenshots, Variants, Manuals, and Keys and help.
**Cheats** where a game has a cheat list: Game Genie, GameShark, Pro Action Replay and memory codes, off until you switch them on.
**Nothing hidden on a narrow screen:** the labels come off first, then the buttons wrap onto another line.

**Emby and Jellyfin.** Sign in with your user name and password, pick yourself from the server's users, or use Quick Connect on Jellyfin. Both can stay signed in; the switch on each tile chooses the one in use.

**Formats browsers give up on.** Files the browser can play are played as they are. MKV is repackaged in the browser, and 10-bit HEVC, AV1, DivX and Xvid are converted live. Dolby Digital, Dolby Digital Plus and DTS are decoded to stereo. When nothing else will do, the player asks your server to convert; Settings chooses Auto, Always or Never.

**Subtitles** drawn by the page, **Up Next** with skipped intros where the server knows them, progress saved back to your server, and silent **widgets** on the wall: clock, weather, trailers, film facts, collection stats and cast.

**Phones and tablets:** the buttons drawn on each device are the buttons you press, a see-through pad appears when a game needs more, rumble games buzz the phone, tilt games follow it, and the site can be added to the home screen.

**Folds:** the Systems menu and Settings open full screen on phones, folds and small tablets, either way up, and every window (Home, Features, Compatibility, Timeline, About) has a close button there.

**Controllers:** A is A on Nintendo-style and Xbox-style pads, players two to four join on their own pads where a game allows it, and every key and button can be changed in Settings. A TV remote's arrows, OK, Back and colour keys work across the site.

**R.O.B., the Robotic Operating Buddy,** has his own place on the wall. Start Gyromite or Stack-Up and a 3D R.O.B. stands beside the game, reads its screen flashes and moves his arms and hands at the real robot's speed. Set out his gyros, trays and blocks with a mouse, a finger or a controller; a spinning gyro on its tray presses the button the game waits for, and Stack-Up checks your blocks against the picture it asked for. Play Time lets you drive him yourself. It runs in the browser, with no add-on to install.
**All 61 classic units play,** each with its own on-screen buttons in close-up view and full screen; the units with a clock start at the right time of day.
**The SM5A units keep time:** their one-second counter ticks every 60.00 frames on 15 of 15 units that can be measured, and their beep is at the right pitch.
**The colour units** (Super Mario Bros. and The Legend of Zelda) run at the panel's 60 frames a second, with their music at its own tempo and clean sound.
**Tetris Jr.,** a 1988 prototype, is rebuilt and playable. No program from it survives, so it is rebuilt rather than emulated.
**Each unit's drawer** opens on a still of its own artwork with its screen running the demo.
**One project licence,** the CrystalWorlds.Media Project Licence 1.1, covers the code and the assets.

**Research and documentation** may be read, cited and quoted in reasonable excerpts with credit (in paid work too), and its facts may be used, with credit, to improve your own projects. It may not be copied wholesale, presented as someone else's own work, or used as the source to build an emulator or a front end (section 3A of the licence).
**The source code** is provided so anyone can check our results. It and the emulator cores may not be used to develop other front-end software (section 3B).

**No AI-built copies and no AI training.** No AI or other automated system may build software from our documentation or source, or be trained on them, and text and data mining is reserved. Repeating our clean-room proof, an AI included, to check our results is allowed (sections 3C to 3E).
**NES:** 182 of the 4,530 games tested do not play yet (73 boot but do not play, 109 show nothing).
**Atari 5200:** with the original BIOS, 11 of 495 games do not play; on our own replacement firmware 454 of 522 files play, and the 32 games that use Atari's own code need the original.
**Atari 7800:** 183 files show nothing without the console's BIOS.
**Atari Lynx:** 20 of 829 games boot but do not play.
**Pokémon mini:** our emulator does not match the console on two of our twelve tests, the save memory and the clock at start-up.
**Plex** is not supported.
